the rude kings of pastoral Garamant] The word ‘rude’ to describe the Garamantes, a tribe identified
with the interior of Libya, is indicative of the classical view that they were backward. See Herodotus,
Histories iv 174 (‘the Garamantes dwell in the wild beasts’ country. They shun the sight and fellowship
of men, and have no weapons of war, nor know how to defend themselves’), and iv 183–4 (where the
tribe is described as twenty days’ journey from Mount Atlas); Pliny, Hist. Nat. v 26 and 36; Lucan,
Pharsalia iv 334–5 (‘Cancrique sub axe,/Qua nudi Garamantes arant’ (‘beneath the sign of Cancer,
where the naked Garamantes plough the earth’)), ix 369 and 460. As noted in Kellett, Suggestions (1923)
117, in ‘rude kings’ there may be a specific reference to Iarbas, an African lord described in Aeneid iv
198 as ‘Hammone satus, rapta Garamantide Nympha’ (‘son of Hammon by a ravished Garamantian
